items.stem: State the two weighings that together give the magnesium's mass in the crucible practical.
items.modelAnswer: Weigh the crucible with its lid first, then again with the magnesium inside — the difference between them is the metal's mass.

items.stem: State the double purpose of lifting the crucible lid during the heating.
items.modelAnswer: Enough air enters for the magnesium to fully oxidise, while the magnesium oxide smoke must not escape.

items.stem: Explain why heating continues until the crucible's mass is constant.
items.modelAnswer: A constant mass shows the maximum mass has been reached — the reaction is complete, with every bit of magnesium oxidised.

items.stem: In a repeat run, 0.48 g of magnesium (Ar 24) is burnt and the oxide collected weighs 0.80 g. Show the moles of Mg and of O, and state the formula the ratio gives.
items.misconceptionClass: mole ratio from crucible data applied
items.modelAnswer: Mg: 0.48 / 24 = 0.02 mol; O: (0.80 - 0.48) / 16 = 0.32 / 16 = 0.02 mol; the ratio is 1 : 1, so the formula is MgO.

items.stem: State the aim of the copper(II) oxide practical.
items.modelAnswer: To find the formula of copper(II) oxide, by reduction of the oxide with methane.

items.stem: State how the oxygen's mass is obtained in the copper oxide practical.
items.modelAnswer: The oxygen's mass is the oxide's mass minus the metal's mass left after the reduction.

items.stem: Explain why the excess methane is burned off at the end of the practical.
items.modelAnswer: Because methane is flammable — burning it off means the flammable gas is not released into the lab.

items.stem: A tube holds 2.40 g of copper(II) oxide; after reduction, 1.92 g of copper remains (Cu 63.5, O 16). Show both mole results and state the formula they give.
items.modelAnswer: Cu: 1.92 / 63.5 = 0.03 mol (about); O: (2.40 - 1.92) / 16 = 0.48 / 16 = 0.03 mol; the ratio is 1 : 1, so the formula is CuO.

items.stem: State what the empirical formula shows.
items.modelAnswer: The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element present.

items.stem: State which class of compound is always written in empirical form.
items.modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are always written as empirical formulae.

items.stem: Explain why ethanoic acid's molecular formula, C2H4O2, and its empirical formula, CH2O, differ.
items.modelAnswer: Because the counts in C2H4O2 share a common factor of two — dividing every count down to the simplest whole-number ratio gives CH2O.

items.stem: A compound analyses as 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen (C 12, H 1, O 16). Run the element-by-element table and state the empirical formula.
items.modelAnswer: C: 40.0 / 12 = 3.33; H: 6.7 / 1 = 6.7; O: 53.3 / 16 = 3.33; dividing by the smallest gives 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH2O.

items.stem: State how the multiplier between the empirical and molecular formulae is obtained.
items.modelAnswer: Divide the molecular formula's mass by the empirical formula's own mass.

items.stem: State what a hydrated salt carries in its crystal structure, and how it is written.
items.modelAnswer: Water molecules, written after a dot — for example CuSO4.5H2O.

items.stem: Explain why the same empirical table still works when the substance is a hydrated salt.
items.modelAnswer: Because the table only needs two substances and their relative formula masses — salt and water replace the elements, and Mr values replace the atomic ones, so the same mole-and-ratio steps run unchanged.

items.stem: A compound's empirical formula is NO2 (N 14, O 16) and its relative formula mass is 92. State the multiplier and the molecular formula.
items.modelAnswer: Empirical mass = 14 + (2 x 16) = 46; 92 / 46 = 2, so the multiplier is 2 and the molecular formula is N2O4.

items.stem: Define solute, solvent and solution.
items.modelAnswer: The solute is the solid that dissolves; the solvent is the liquid it dissolves into; together they form the solution.

items.stem: State the two unit families concentration is quoted in, and which of them is the more useful.
items.modelAnswer: Grams per dm3 (g / dm3) or moles per dm3 (mol / dm3) — the moles measure is the more useful of the two.

items.stem: Explain why a volume in cm3 must be converted before any concentration working begins.
items.modelAnswer: Because concentration units are per dm3, so a cm3 volume must be divided by 1000 before it enters the sum.

items.stem: A solution holds 0.1 mol of solute in 250 cm3 of solution. Convert the volume, then state the concentration in mol / dm3.
State the relationship between moles, concentration and volume that the formula triangle encodes.
items.modelAnswer: Moles of solute equal concentration multiplied by volume, with the volume in dm3 — cover the one you want on the triangle.

items.stem: State how to find the volume of a solution from its moles and concentration.
items.modelAnswer: Volume equals the moles divided by the concentration.

items.stem: Explain why a titration result needs the balanced equation's ratio.
items.modelAnswer: Because the titration gives the moles of one solution only — the balanced equation's ratio scales those moles across to the other solution.

items.stem: 5.0 g of sodium hydroxide (Na 23, O 16, H 1) dissolves to make 250 cm3 of solution. Convert the mass to moles and the volume to dm3, then state the concentration.
items.modelAnswer: Mr of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40; moles = 5.0 / 40 = 0.125 mol; volume = 250 / 1000 = 0.25 dm3; concentration = 0.125 / 0.25 = 0.5 mol / dm3.

items.stem: State the molar gas volume at RTP in both units.
items.modelAnswer: 24 dm3, which is the same as 24,000 cm3.

items.stem: State what RTP stands for and the values it stands for.
items.modelAnswer: Room temperature and pressure — 20 degrees Celsius and one atmosphere.

items.stem: Explain why 24,000 rather than 24 does the dividing when a volume is given in cm3.
items.modelAnswer: Because the molar volume is 24 dm3, and 1 dm3 = 1,000 cm3, so in cm3 the same molar volume is 24,000.

items.stem: State the volume, in dm3, occupied by 2.5 mol of nitrogen gas at RTP.
State the two steps that turn a gas's mass into its volume.
items.modelAnswer: Convert the mass to moles with Mr, then multiply the moles by 24.

items.stem: State what gives the ratio of gas volumes directly, without any Mr working.
items.modelAnswer: The coefficients of the balanced equation, under Avogadro's law.

items.stem: In C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O, explain why one volume of propane needs five volumes of oxygen.
items.modelAnswer: Because under Avogadro's law the coefficient ratio is the volume ratio — propane's coefficient is 1 and oxygen's is 5, so the gases react 1 : 5 by volume.

items.stem: In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O (steam), 200 cm3 of hydrogen reacts fully with 100 cm3 of oxygen, both measured at RTP. State the total volume of steam formed.
items.modelAnswer: The coefficient ratio is 2 : 1 : 2, so 200 cm3 of hydrogen gives 200 cm3 of steam (using exactly the 100 cm3 of oxygen supplied).

items.stem: Name the three noble gases the note names for electronic structures.
items.modelAnswer: Helium, neon and argon.

items.stem: State what every metal atom does in ion forming, and what every non-metal atom does.
items.modelAnswer: Every metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positive ion; every non-metal gains electrons and becomes a negative ion.

items.stem: Explain why an atom that gives up electrons ends up with a positive charge.
items.modelAnswer: Because electrons are negative — losing them leaves more protons than electrons, so the particle's overall charge is positive.

items.stem: An oxygen atom has 8 electrons (2,6) and gains 2 more. State the ion's charge and the noble-gas structure it now matches.
items.modelAnswer: The ion carries a 2- charge and matches the 2,8 structure of neon.

items.stem: Define a cation.
items.modelAnswer: A cation is a positive ion that forms when an atom loses electrons, leaving more protons than electrons.

items.stem: State the charge on the magnesium ion and on the bromide ion from the lesson's examples.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium loses 2 electrons for a 2+ charge; bromine gains 1 electron for a 1- charge.

items.stem: Explain why an anion carries a negative charge.
items.modelAnswer: Because gaining electrons leaves more electrons than protons, so the overall charge is negative.

items.stem: Aluminium (Group 3) reacts with sulfur (Group 6). State which element forms the cation, which forms the anion, and each ion's charge.
items.modelAnswer: Aluminium is the cation at 3+ (a Group 3 metal donating its three outer electrons); sulfur is the anion at 2- (a Group 6 non-metal receiving two electrons).

items.stem: State what a compound ion is, and what its formula demands.
items.modelAnswer: An ion made from more than one element — its formula must be learned as given.

items.stem: State what kind of ion forms when an atom's outer electron count sits below four.
items.modelAnswer: A positive ion — the atom donates its outer electrons.

items.stem: Explain why a Group 7 atom ends up carrying a 1- charge.
items.modelAnswer: Because a Group 7 atom has seven outer electrons — more than four — so it receives one electron to complete the shell, ending with one extra electron and a 1- charge.

items.stem: A neutral atom has the configuration 2,8,3. State whether it donates or receives electrons, and the charge of the ion it forms.
items.modelAnswer: It has 3 outer electrons — fewer than four — so it donates all three and forms a 3+ ion.

items.stem: Name the five compound ions the table says to know, with their charges.
items.modelAnswer: Hydroxide OH-, ammonium NH4+, carbonate CO3 2-, nitrate NO3- and sulfate SO4 2-.

items.stem: State the ion that hydrogen rides as in the common-ions table.
items.modelAnswer: H+, alongside the metal ions.

items.stem: Explain why iron appears twice in the common-ions table.
items.modelAnswer: Because iron forms two different positive ions — Fe2+ and Fe3+ — depending on how many electrons it loses.

items.stem: A compound contains potassium ions and carbonate ions. State each ion's charge and the overall formula of the compound.
items.modelAnswer: Potassium (Group 1) gives K+; carbonate is CO3 2-; two K+ ions balance one carbonate, so the formula is K2CO3.
